title: Models for improvising: Armstrong, Lunceford's trumpeter and Red Nichols
summary: He learned solos from records, combined them into his own ideas, and became known for high notes and endurance.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Now, who were the people that you really emulated during this period? I mean, from the radio or whatever. Did you have any ideas of those people that you mentioned before, that you were inspired greatly by Louis Armstrong, of course, in terms of that.
But, in terms of improvisation, and, first of all, when did you first begin to improvise and work on your solos like that, and who were some of the people that inspired you?

Well, I would have to say that after Louis Armstrong, then I started listening to Stevenson, I think his name is, with Jimmy Lunceford. See, I was still in school when Jimmy Lunceford got there. So, when I was, they used to do a lot of broadcasting out of the Cotton Club.

And then from there, I started kind of getting myself together especially from records. There's some names I can't remember, trumpet players on there. I'm thinking. But, I knew a Red Nichols during that time. I used to try and play some of those solos. And then, after I got those solos, and after learning them, then I started playing them like I wanted to play during those years.
When you say playing like you wanted to play, what was that?
Yeah. What was that like? How did you go about that?

Well, I took some of theirs, a little of this. I took a little from everybody, you know, and put it together. And then, that started me that way. Then, after I got that way, I started going for myself.
And how did other people react to what you were doing?
Well, as far as I remember, they liked it. Yeah, cause after that,

they started, I started going for high notes. I started doing a lot of high notes, and then they started calling me "Iron Lung" during those years cause I could last so long. I could play all day without getting tired. That's how they would use to go for me pretty good. They always sent for me.
And you didn't practice anything in particular that you can remember that gave you that kind of endurance?
No. I'd just stand in the band room all the time and keep practicing. You know, and I'd keep blowing. I loved it. You know?
So, that's just, maybe the sports helped. It gave me a lot of wind maybe.
